seriesTitle: The Lantern Mender of Pell Street
title: Somebody Will Want It
blurb: Ada takes a hem note to the Provost and the square hears the rest. Some truths clear the air; the next one is under the floor.

blocks.text: The Provost's step was cold through her boots, and first bell had not finished ringing.
Ada stood with the hem note in her fist and talked to the door.

"This is a note," she said. "It was in a hem. It's dated Flood Night. It's in the hand of Ines Fane, and her sister says you can read it." She breathed. "That's all. That's all you say. You do not say what you—"
She shut her mouth so hard her teeth clicked.
"Paper," she told the door. "Just the paper."
The door opened before she could knock.
Provost Harrow stood in it, coat buttoned to the chin, black gloves on. Behind her the hall was dark but for one lamp.
"Nobody stands on my step at first bell talking to themselves, Mender, unless they have something for the record." She stepped aside. "Come in. Do not speak until I tell you that you may."
The hall was colder inside than out. It always was. Ada's boots rang on the stone, and somewhere high up a window rattled in its frame.
Odile had pressed the slip into her hand at the blue door an hour before. "Take it to whoever needs it. Ines would have."
Harrow sat at the long table and held out one gloved hand.
Ada put the slip in it.
Harrow unfolded it under the lamp. Ada watched her eyes go along the line once. Then to the date. Then along the line again.
If the lamps go dark tonight, don't blame the girl.

Ada knew the Provost's pauses by now, one before every concession. This one went on. Ada counted it under her breath. Four. Five. In its cabinet in the wall, Harrow's lantern burned white-gold behind the glass. Nine. Ten.
Eleven.
"Where was this found?" said Harrow.
Ada kept her mouth shut.

"Yes," said Harrow. "Quite right. I told you not to." She laid the slip flat and put her gloved hand beside it, not on it. "Mender. You have my leave to speak what you saw in my lantern. All of it. Under the charter. So noted."
Ada looked at the cabinet and waited for the red.
It didn't come.

"A desk," she said. "Lamplight. Rain on a high window. A clock ticking, slow and heavy. I'd never heard it tick." Her voice stayed level. Short sentences, like reading off a meter. "A gloved hand writing. 'Order under the charter.' 'The lower sluice.' 'At once.' Sluice again, underlined. Signed, R. Harrow. Through the window, every lamp on the lower quay was dark. Lower on the page, smaller: 'Lower-quay lamps unlit at ninth bell. Whose watch?'" She swallowed. "Then the pen stopped. And you said, 'Not tonight.'"
The window rattled again.
"Two things," said Harrow at last. "The order. And the question I did not ask."
Secrets held: 2. Not a riddle, then. A count. Two things one woman had chosen to keep.

"And then I did not ask the next night," said Harrow, "or the next, for ten years." She looked down at the slip. "This woman knew enough to warn someone. I knew enough to ask. Neither of us was heard." The pause again, shorter. "That ends at fourth bell."
By fourth bell the square was full for market, and then it was quiet, which Ada had never heard it be.
The clock tower stood over them, face dark, hands still. A cart wheel creaked once and stopped.
Harrow stood on the hall steps, gloves on. Emrys stood one step below with the hall's minute book open on his forearm, very pale.
"Under the charter," said Harrow, "I make a statement for the record."
Nobody moved.

"On Flood Night, at ninth bell, I ordered the lower sluice opened. Had it stayed shut, the upper town would have flooded. I knew that if I opened it, the canal quarter would flood instead." "I would not send anyone else to do it. I signed out the key myself. I opened the sluice. I stayed in the sluice house until first bell and listened to what it did."
Somewhere in the crowd a woman made a small sound.
"Eleven people drowned on the lower quay. That was my order."

Ada found Odile at the edge of the crowd, one hand flat on her pincushion, Tobias beside her. Further back, by the bun stall, stood Hester with a basket on her arm. She had been humming when Ada came into the square. She wasn't now.

"I also wrote, that night, that the lower-quay lamps were unlit at ninth bell," said Harrow. "I asked whose watch it was. I did not pursue it." She lifted the slip. "This was found last night in a hem. It is in the hand of Ines Fane, who drowned that night. Her sister has given leave for it to be read." She read it, plain and clipped. "'If the lamps go dark tonight, don't blame the girl.'"
The square took that in like a held breath.
"Somebody knew," said Harrow. "I am pursuing it now. Anyone who carried a lamplighter's pole on Flood Night will come to the hall. So noted." Then: "Registrar."
Emrys came up a step and held out the book and the pen.
Harrow looked at the pen. Then she drew off her right glove, finger by finger, and then the left.
"A confession is signed by the hand that did it," she said. "Not by the office."
She turned her hands over to take the pen, and Ada saw her palms.
Pale. Lined. A callus where a pen sat. An old ink stain down the side of one finger.
No silver. Not a thread of it.
Hot glass marks the hand that breaks it. Silver, and for life.
Harrow signed, quick and hard, the same R. Harrow Ada had watched a gloved hand write in a lantern. Then she drew her gloves on and went inside, and the door shut like a book closing.
Emrys came down the steps. "Her palms," he said, low.
"I saw."
"Clean." He took his spectacles off. "For the record, I had the whole case on the back of a bun paper."
"I know. I added to it."
"Then who?"
Ada didn't answer. There was a sum somewhere at the back of her head, and she left it there unfinished, the way she had in the oil store.
Hester was working through the crowd, pressing buns into hands without a word. She put one into Ada's, gloved fingers brushing her wrist, and moved on.
Ada looked at the bun. Not at the glove.
She spent the afternoon with Barnaby's tin tipped out on the bench, sorting canal glass by colour and by feel.
Most of it was cold as the canal. Seven pieces weren't: pale green like old bottle glass, and faintly warm in the palm, like a cup just put down.
Emrys came at ninth bell with the Register under his arm and stood where he always stood, hands behind his back, without being asked.
"Seven," he said.
"Seven."
Ninth bell rang across the water, deep and slow, and the readout came up over the bench in pale gold.
GLASS. And beneath it: INCOMPLETE.
The line of light ran from piece to piece, edge to edge, all seven, and then off the last and across the bench, pointing at nothing. The bar came up empty, with its notch cut from the far end.
"Same as Pike," she said. "Short the last shard. It can be closed."

She set the first two pieces together. Glass clicked on glass. In the frame, the wick hissed. She worked edge to edge, like testing a run of cable, and counted under her breath. At twenty the bar was a third full. At thirty-eight it reached the notch and stopped, clean as a measurement.
And the word over the bench changed.
GLASS went thin and bright and gave way, and the letters that came up behind it were warmer, the colour of a struck match.
FLAME.
She didn't say it aloud this time. Emrys was watching her face.
Then the memory came.

A low room smelling of tar and hemp. Rain loud on a slate roof. An old woman with a white plait knelt by her bed and pushed a packed carpet bag underneath it, all the way to the wall. Water was coming under the door in a thin bright sheet.
"First bell," the old woman said, to nobody, in a voice like a gate that wanted oil. "Fog road, first bell, and none of them the wiser."
Shouting outside. Far off, down towards the lower quay. The old woman got up, stiff, took a coil of rope from its peg, hitched it over her shoulder, and opened the door into the water.
The memory ran out ragged as a torn page. At the edge of it, for half a breath: a dark glove. Fingers closing.
Ada let go of the bench.
Emrys had the Register open already, at Rope Walk, where a line had stood blank all the years he had kept the book. It wasn't blank now.
"Rook, Nan," he read, very quietly. "Ropemaker. Rope Walk." His finger moved to the right-hand column. "Drowned. Flood Night." He straightened. "Three."
On the bench the lantern had made itself: green glass, whole but for a ragged gap low on one side, and a small, low, steady flame. Ada set it on the shelf beside Pike's.
Emrys didn't ask what she had seen. He had stopped asking.
"This morning," he said instead. "'Whose watch.' That was what you couldn't tell me. In the record room. At Odile's table."
"Since the night in the hall."
"You carried that the whole time." He put his spectacles back on. "For the record, I would rather you hadn't had to."
"For the record," said Ada, "so would I."
He very nearly smiled.
She took the brown paper list from the drawer. Rule two. Then she went looking for what had gone.

Her mother's kitchen: there. The front gate with its loose hinge. Red brick, third from the corner. She walked to the end of the street in her head and looked up at the sign on the wall, and the sign was blank. Like a Register line.
She wrote: 7. The street I grew up on.
Emrys could read it upside down. She didn't turn it away. He put his hand flat on the bench, not quite near hers, and left it there until first bell.
Hester came at first bell with currant buns and a twist of butter, and something under her oilskin that she set on the bench with both gloved hands.
A lantern. New glass, plain brass, the wick trimmed and never lit.
"Glazier on the bridge owed me," said Hester. "Don't ask what for." She split a bun, buttered it with her gloves on, and pushed it across. "Eat that first."
Ada looked at the lantern. "Hester."

"Heard her this morning, didn't I. Whole square did." Hester was not humming. "Lot of truth for one day, petal. Thought the day could do with one nice thing in it." She took a taper from her pocket and struck it on the bench edge. It hissed. "You've been nobody long enough."
"It costs you a memory."
"A good one, love. I had a few." She opened the little door in the lantern and held the taper to the wick.
"Which one?"
"Don't you worry which. That's the point of giving, my duck. You don't get to see the wrapping."
The wick didn't take. Hester's face went still and very far away, and for a moment she looked younger than Ada had ever seen her.
Then the flame came up out of nothing, like a breath let go.

It was small and clear, the colour of a kitchen window seen from the street at night. Ada felt it, not in her hands but under her breastbone, the way you feel a door shut behind you when you're finally in.
Hester blinked, and smiled, and was Hester again. "There. Now if you walk into that fog, somebody'll miss you."
Over the new lantern, faint as breath on a window, the readout came up by itself: FLAME.
Ada set it on the windowsill. Hester went off down Pell Street with her ladder, putting out the lamps one by one.
She wasn't humming. Ada noticed, and told herself it was early.
She was pushing Barnaby's tin back under the old mender's bench when the board moved under her knee.
A hollow knock, and a give. Every house Ada had ever run a cable through had one board somebody had lifted and never nailed back.
She took the knife from the bench and worked it into the gap. Old nails squealed. The board came up.
Between the joists, dry as a biscuit, lay a parcel in oilcloth tied with string. On the oilcloth, in a hard right slant, underlined twice: Somebody will want it.
She cut the string.
A long, narrow book with a cracked spine. On the cover, in worn gold: LAMPLIGHTERS' LOG.
Paper doesn't swim, Hester had said. It went down with the flood.
Ada turned the pages. Rosters, week on week, names in columns, street by street. She turned faster, towards the date she knew.
The Flood Night page was gone, torn out close to the spine, leaving a ragged stub.
Caught in the tear, fine as a wick, was a thread of black glove leather.
